A common instance is the in-sample\n32\terror\n33\t\n34\t$ E_(i n)(bold(w)) eq.def 1/N sum_(i=1)^N e(h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i), y_i) $\n35\t\n36\twhich averages the pointwise error of a hypothesis $h_(bold(w))$ over $N$\n37\ttraining examples $(bold(x)_i, y_i)$.\n38\t\n39\tTwo broad strategies exist for finding the minimizer. The second is a #emph[numerical approach]:\n44\tuse an iterative method that updates $bold(w)$ step by step until $J(bold(w))$\n45\treaches its minimum. Gradient descent is the prototypical example. A numerical\n46\tmethod remains applicable even when an analytical solution exists, making it the\n47\tmore general-purpose tool, and it scales naturally to the high-dimensional\n48\tparameter spaces encountered in modern models.\n49\t\n50\t@fig:gradientdescent2 illustrates how gradient descent iteratively moves toward\n51\ta minimum of the objective surface.\n52\t\n53\t#figure(\n54\t  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_2.png\", width: 80%),\n55\t  caption: [Gradient descent 2],\n56\t  kind: \"figure\",\n57\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n58\t  placement: auto,\n59\t) <fig:gradientdescent2>\n60\t\n61\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:43 '* Gradient Descent: Intuition'\n62\t// Slide: Gradient Descent: Intuition\n63\t#strong[Gradient Descent: Intuition]\n64\t\n65\tImagine standing on a hilly surface with the goal of reaching the lowest point.\n66\tHow do you get there? At each position, you look around to assess the slope in\n67\tevery direction, then take a step along the steepest downhill direction. You\n68\trepeat this process until you arrive at a point where no further descent is\n69\tpossible. This intuitive procedure is precisely what gradient descent formalizes\n70\tfor mathematical optimization, as @fig:gradientdescent1 illustrates.\n71\t\n72\t#figure(\n73\t  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_1.png\", width: 80%),\n74\t  caption: [Gradient descent 1],\n75\t  kind: \"figure\",\n76\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n77\t  placement: auto,\n78\t) <fig:gradientdescent1>\n79\t\n80\t#strong[Gradient descent] is a general technique for minimizing\n81\ttwice-differentiable functions. Starting from an initial guess, the algorithm\n82\titeratively adjusts its parameters by moving in the direction of the negative\n83\tgradient (the direction of steepest decrease). In the general case, gradient\n84\tdescent converges to a #emph[local minimum], a point that is lower than all\n85\tnearby points but not necessarily the lowest point overall. However, when the\n86\tobjective function $J(bold(w))$ is convex, every local minimum is also the\n87\tglobal minimum, so gradient descent is guaranteed to find the best possible\n88\tsolution. Common models whose loss functions are convex include logistic\n89\tregression and linear regression, which is one reason these models are so widely\n90\tused in practice: their optimization landscape contains no misleading valleys or\n91\tplateaus.\n92\t\n93\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:73 '# Gradient Descent'\n94\t// Slide: Gradient Descent\n95\t#strong[Gradient Descent]\n96\t\n97\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:75 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)'\n98\t// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)\n99\t#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)]\n100\t\n101\tConsider the contour plot of a loss function $E_{\"in\"}$ over weight space.\n102\tGradient descent begins from an initial point $bold(w)(0)$, which might be\n103\tchosen randomly or set to the origin. At each step, the algorithm moves a fixed\n104\tdistance $eta$ (the learning rate) through weight space:\n105\t\n106\t$ bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) + eta hat(bold(v)) $\n107\t\n108\twhere $hat(bold(v))$ is a unit vector indicating the direction of the step. The\n109\tgoal is to choose $hat(bold(v))$ so that $E_{\"in\"}(bold(w))$ decreases as much\n110\tas possible.\n111\t\n112\tTo see which direction accomplishes this, examine the change in the error:\n113\t\n114\t$\n115\t  Delta E_{\"in\"} &= E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t + 1)) - E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t)) \\\n116\t  &= E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t) + eta hat(bold(v))) - E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t)) \\\n117\t  &approx eta nabla E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v)) + O(eta^2)\n118\t$\n119\t\n120\tThe last line follows from a first-order Taylor expansion around $bold(w)(t)$.\n121\tStandard gradient descent retains only the $O(eta)$ term and discards\n122\thigher-order contributions. Because $eta$ is a positive scalar, making\n123\t$Delta E_{\"in\"}$ as negative as possible requires choosing $hat(bold(v))$ to\n124\tminimize the inner product $nabla E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v))$; the unit\n125\tvector that achieves this points in the direction opposite the gradient. More\n126\tadvanced methods such as #emph[conjugate gradient] retain the $O(eta^2)$ term as\n127\twell, which allows them to account for curvature information and often converge\n128\tfaster, though at a higher per-step cost.\n129\t\n130\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:107 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)'\n131\t// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)\n132\t#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)]\n133\t\n134\tThe change in the in-sample error $E_(i n)$ when moving along a unit direction\n135\t$hat(bold(v))$ is approximately\n136\t\n137\t$ Delta E_(i n) approx eta nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v)) $\n138\t\n139\tThis expression is a first-order Taylor approximation: the error shift is\n140\tproportional to the learning rate $eta$ and to how well the step direction\n141\t$hat(bold(v))$ aligns with the gradient. The scalar product $Delta E_(i n)$\n142\treaches its most negative value when $hat(bold(v))$ points exactly opposite to\n143\tthe gradient, that is, when\n144\t\n145\t$\n146\t  hat(bold(v)) = - frac(nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)), \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|)\n147\t$\n148\t\n149\tAt that choice the change equals $- eta \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|$, the\n150\tsteepest possible decrease for a step of size $eta$.\n151\t\n152\tSubstituting this optimal direction back into the weight update gives the full\n153\trule for the #strong[change in weights]:\n154\t\n155\t$\n156\t  Delta bold(w) &= bold(w)(t + 1) - bold(w)(t) \\\n157\t  &= eta hat(bold(v)) \\\n158\t  &= - eta frac(nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)), \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|)\n159\t$\n160\t\n161\tEach iteration therefore moves the weight vector a fixed distance $eta$ in\n162\twhichever direction reduces the error most steeply. The method is called\n163\t#strong[gradient descent] precisely because it descends along the gradient of\n164\tthe objective function, following the locally steepest downhill path at every\n165\tstep.\n166\t\n167\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:133 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)'\n168\t// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)\n169\t#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)]\n170\t\n171\tThe gradient descent update formula specifies how each component of the weight\n172\tvector changes at every step. The full vector update is\n173\t\n174\t$\n175\t  bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) - eta frac(nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t)), \\|nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t))\\|)\n176\t$\n177\t\n178\tand the corresponding per-coordinate form for the $j$-th weight is\n179\t\n180\t$\n181\t  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - eta frac(1, \\|nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t))\\|) frac(partial E_(i n)(bold(w)), partial w_j)\n182\t$\n183\t\n184\tEach weight moves in the direction that locally reduces the in-sample error,\n185\tscaled by the learning rate $eta$ and normalized by the gradient's magnitude. A\n186\tcritical detail is that the update of all components must be\n187\t#emph[simultaneous]: every partial derivative is evaluated at the current point\n188\t$bold(w)(t)$ before any component is changed, so no single coordinate's new\n189\tvalue contaminates the computation of another's update within the same step.\n190\t\n191\tAn #strong[iteration] of gradient descent refers to one complete application of\n192\tthis update rule, producing a new weight vector from the current one. Counting\n193\titerations gives a natural measure of computational effort and is the basis for\n194\tconvergence criteria and stopping conditions.\n195\t\n196\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:153 '* Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria'\n197\t// Slide: Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria\n198\t#strong[Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria]\n199\t\n200\tWhen should gradient descent stop? In theory, the algorithm terminates when the\n201\tchange in the in-sample error reaches zero, $Delta E_(\"in\") = bold(0)$. In\n202\tpractice, however, this exact condition may never be satisfied numerically due\n203\tto finite floating-point precision and the iterative nature of the updates. Two\n204\tpractical stopping criteria are commonly used instead:\n205\t\n206\t- #emph[Threshold on variation]: stop when the change in $E_(\"in\")$ falls below\n207\t  a small threshold, $Delta E_(\"in\") < theta$.\n208\t- #emph[Iteration budget]: stop after a predetermined number of iterations,\n209\t  regardless of whether full convergence has been reached.\n210\t\n211\tMonitoring the optimization process also differs between theory and practice. In\n212\ttheory, gradient descent requires only the derivatives of the cost function\n213\t$J(bold(w))$ to determine each update step. In practice, it is wise to\n214\tperiodically recompute the cost function $J(bold(w))$ itself and verify that it\n215\tis actually decreasing. If the cost plateaus or begins to increase, that signals\n216\ta problem: the learning rate may be too large, causing the iterates to\n217\tovershoot, or the algorithm may have reached a region of the loss surface where\n218\tthe gradient provides poor guidance. Periodically logging $J(bold(w))$ provides\n219\ta simple but effective diagnostic for catching these issues early.\n220\t\n221\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:167 '# Tuning Gradient Descent'\n222\t// Slide: Tuning Gradient Descent\n223\t#strong[Tuning Gradient Descent]\n224\t\n225\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:169 '* Choosing the Learning Rate'\n226\t// Slide: Choosing the Learning Rate\n227\t#strong[Choosing the Learning Rate]\n228\t\n229\tConsider a one-dimensional convex function whose minimum we seek via gradient\n230\tdescent. The behavior of the algorithm depends critically on the choice of\n231\tlearning rate $eta$.\n232\t\n233\tWhen $eta$ is too small, the linear approximation of $E_(i n)$ remains effective\n234\tat each step, so every update does move downhill, but the steps are tiny and\n235\tconvergence to the minimum requires a large number of iterations.\n236\t@fig:gradientdescent3a illustrates this slow, cautious trajectory.\n237\t\n238\t#figure(\n239\t  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3a.png\", width: 80%),\n240\t  caption: [Gradient descent 3a],\n241\t  kind: \"figure\",\n242\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n243\t  placement: auto,\n244\t) <fig:gradientdescent3a>\n245\t\n246\tWhen $eta$ is too large, the linear approximation breaks down because\n247\thigher-order terms in the Taylor expansion dominate the actual function values.\n248\tInstead of descending smoothly, the iterates overshoot the minimum and bounce\n249\tback and forth across the valley, potentially diverging altogether.\n250\t@fig:gradientdescent3b shows this oscillatory behavior.\n251\t\n252\t#figure(\n253\t  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3b.png\", width: 80%),\n254\t  caption: [Gradient descent 3b],\n255\t  kind: \"figure\",\n256\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n257\t  placement: auto,\n258\t) <fig:gradientdescent3b>\n259\t\n260\tA natural idea is to vary $eta$ over the course of optimization. Starting with a\n261\tlarger learning rate lets the algorithm make rapid initial progress, and then\n262\tgradually reducing $eta$ as a function of the iteration count allows it to\n263\tsettle into a tighter neighborhood of the minimum. Smaller learning rates in\n264\tlater stages can even help the optimizer find a better local minimum in\n265\tnon-convex landscapes. The tradeoff is that a learning-rate schedule introduces\n266\tan additional hyperparameter (or family of hyperparameters, such as a decay rate\n267\tand a decay schedule) that must itself be tuned, adding complexity to the\n268\ttraining pipeline. @fig:gradientdescent3c depicts the effect of a well-chosen\n269\tadaptive schedule, where early large steps give way to finer adjustments near\n270\tthe optimum.\n271\t\n272\t#figure(\n273\t  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3c.png\", width: 80%),\n274\t  caption: [Gradient descent 3c],\n275\t  kind: \"figure\",\n276\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n277\t  placement: auto,\n278\t) <fig:gradientdescent3c>\n279\t\n280\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:202 '* Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate'\n281\t// Slide: Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate\n282\t#strong[Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate]\n283\t\n284\tWhen using #strong[gradient descent with a fixed learning rate], every update\n285\tmoves the same distance through weight space regardless of how steep the surface\n286\tis. The update rule normalizes the gradient so that only its direction matters:\n287\t\n288\t$ Delta bold(w) = - eta frac(nabla J, \\|nabla J\\|) $\n289\t\n290\tThis keeps the step size constant at $eta$, but that uniformity creates a\n291\tproblem. On steep regions of the loss surface, a fixed step may be too small,\n292\tmaking progress painfully slow. Near a minimum, where the surface flattens out,\n293\tthat same fixed step may be too large, causing the optimizer to overshoot and\n294\tbounce back and forth across the valley instead of settling in.\n295\t\n296\tTo converge quickly, the learning rate should adapt to the local geometry. The\n297\toptimizer should take large steps when the gradient is large (the surface is\n298\tsteep and far from a minimum) and small steps when the gradient is small (the\n299\tsurface is nearly flat and close to a minimum). In other words, the ideal\n300\tlearning rate is proportional to the gradient magnitude: $eta prop \\|nabla J\\|$.\n301\t\n302\t#strong[Gradient descent with a variable learning rate] achieves exactly this by\n303\tdropping the normalization and using the raw gradient directly:\n304\t\n305\t$ Delta bold(w) = - eta nabla J $\n306\t\n307\tBecause the gradient vector $nabla J$ is not divided by its own norm, its\n308\tmagnitude naturally scales the step size. When the surface is steep,\n309\t$\\|nabla J\\|$ is large and the update moves farther; when the surface is gentle,\n310\t$\\|nabla J\\|$ is small and the update shrinks. The scalar $eta$ still controls\n311\tthe overall scale, but the gradient's magnitude now acts as a built-in adaptive\n312\tfactor. This simple change gives the optimizer the variable-rate behavior needed\n313\tfor efficient convergence: aggressive movement far from the optimum and cautious\n314\trefinement near it.\n315\t\n316\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:222 '* Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent'\n317\t// Slide: Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent\n318\t#strong[Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent]\n319\t\n320\tUnscaled features distort the error surface. When one feature ranges from 1 to\n321\t1000 while another ranges from 0.01 to 1, the level sets of $E_\"in\" (bold(w))$\n322\tbecome elongated ellipses rather than circles. A single learning rate cannot\n323\tserve both directions well: it is too large along the steep, short-axis\n324\tdirection (causing the updates to overshoot and bounce) and too small along the\n325\tflat, long-axis direction (causing the optimizer to crawl). The result is slow,\n326\tunstable convergence that zigzags across the narrow valley instead of heading\n327\tstraight for the minimum.\n328\t\n329\tThe fix is to rescale every feature so that all of them span comparable ranges\n330\tbefore training begins. Two common choices are #emph[min-max scaling], which\n331\tmaps each feature to the interval $[0, 1]$, and #emph[standardization], which\n332\tcenters each feature at zero with unit variance. Either approach reshapes the\n333\telongated ellipses into something much closer to circles, so a single learning\n334\trate works reasonably well in every direction and gradient descent converges\n335\tfaster and more smoothly.\n336\t\n337\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:236 '# Scaling to Large Datasets'\n338\t// Slide: Scaling to Large Datasets\n339\t#strong[Scaling to Large Datasets]\n340\t\n341\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:238 '* Issues with Batch Gradient Descent'\n342\t// Slide: Issues with Batch Gradient Descent\n343\t#strong[Issues with Batch Gradient Descent]\n344\t\n345\tConsider the squared error over $N$ training samples, defined as\n346\t\n347\t$\n348\t  E_(i n)(bold(w)) triangleq 1 / N sum_(i=1)^N (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i) - y_i)^2\n349\t$\n350\t\n351\tThis measures the average discrepancy between the hypothesis $h_(bold(w))$ and\n352\tthe observed targets across the entire dataset. Minimizing it drives the model\n353\ttoward a set of weights that fits the training data well.\n354\t\n355\t#strong[Batch Gradient Descent (BGD)] updates the weight vector by stepping in\n356\tthe direction opposite to the normalized gradient of the in-sample error:\n357\t\n358\t$ bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) - eta frac(nabla E_(i n), \\|nabla E_(i n)\\|) $\n359\t\n360\tWriting out the coordinate-level update for the squared error loss makes the\n361\tcomputation concrete. Each weight component $w_j$ changes according to\n362\t\n363\t$\n364\t  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - eta frac(2, N) sum_(i=1)^N (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i) - y_i) frac(partial h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i), partial w_j)\n365\t$\n366\t\n367\tThe inner sum sweeps over every training example, accumulating the product of\n368\tthe current residual and the local sensitivity of the hypothesis to $w_j$. Only\n369\tafter that full pass does the algorithm take a single step.\n370\t\n371\tThat full-dataset requirement is the chief drawback of batch gradient descent.\n372\tWhen $N$ is large (say, $N = 10^6$), every single weight update demands a\n373\tgradient evaluation that touches all $10^6$ examples, making each iteration\n374\tcomputationally expensive. The entire dataset must also reside in memory at\n375\tonce, which can be prohibitive for large-scale problems. These costs motivate\n376\tthe stochastic and mini-batch variants discussed next, which trade a noisier\n377\tgradient estimate for dramatically cheaper per-step computation.\n378\t\n379\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:263 '* Stochastic Gradient Descent'\n380\t// Slide: Stochastic Gradient Descent\n381\t#strong[Stochastic Gradient Descent]\n382\t\n383\t#strong[Stochastic Gradient Descent] (SGD) updates the weights using only a\n384\tsingle training example chosen at random, rather than computing the gradient\n385\tover the entire dataset. This makes each update far cheaper, which is especially\n386\tvaluable when the training set is large.\n387\t\n388\tThe procedure works as follows:\n389\t\n390\t1. Pick one example $(bold(x)_n, y_n)$ at random from the training set.\n391\t2. Compute the gradient of the loss for that single example,\n392\t  $nabla e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n)$, and form the weight update\n393\t  $Delta bold(w) = -eta nabla e$.\n394\t3. Apply the update to each weight:\n395\t\n396\t$\n397\t  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - 2 eta (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_t) - y_t) frac(partial h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_t), partial w_j)\n398\t$\n399\t\n400\tBecause each step relies on a single randomly selected example, the path SGD\n401\ttraces through weight space is noisy: it does not follow the smooth trajectory\n402\tof batch gradient descent but instead oscillates, sometimes moving away from the\n403\toptimum before correcting course. Near a local minimum the updates do not settle\n404\tcleanly; they bounce around the basin rather than converging to a fixed point.\n405\t\n406\tDespite this apparent randomness, SGD works because the gradient $nabla e$ is a\n407\tfunction of a random variable $bold(x)_n$, and its expected value equals the\n408\tfull-batch gradient. Concretely:\n409\t\n410\t$\n411\t  bb(E)[nabla e] = frac(1, N) sum nabla e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n) = nabla frac(1, N) sum e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n) = nabla E_(\"in\")\n412\t$\n413\t\n414\tIn other words, although any single SGD step may point in a direction that\n415\tdiffers from the true gradient, on average the steps point the same way as the\n416\tbatch gradient. Over many iterations the random deviations cancel out, and the\n417\talgorithm makes steady progress toward a minimum of the in-sample error. The\n418\toscillation that is a drawback in the short term actually confers a benefit: the\n419\tnoise helps SGD escape shallow local minima that batch descent might get trapped\n420\tin, often leading to solutions that generalize better.\n421\t\n422\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:294 '* Mini-Batch Gradient Descent'\n423\t// Slide: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent\n424\t#strong[Mini-Batch Gradient Descent]\n425\t\n426\t#strong[Mini-batch gradient descent] brings together characteristics of both\n427\t#emph[batch] and #emph[stochastic gradient descent]. Rather than computing the\n428\tgradient over the entire training set (as in batch gradient descent) or from a\n429\tsingle example (as in stochastic gradient descent), mini-batch gradient descent\n430\tuses a subset of $b$ examples to compute each update to the current weight\n431\tvector. Here $b$ is called the #emph[batch size], and common choices are\n432\t$b = 32$ or $b = 64$. This middle ground reduces the variance of parameter\n433\tupdates compared to the single-sample stochastic approach, while remaining far\n434\tmore computationally tractable per step than a full-batch computation.\n435\tMini-batch updates also benefit from hardware-level parallelism on modern GPUs,\n436\twhich are optimized for matrix operations on moderately sized batches. The\n437\tchoice of batch size introduces its own tradeoff: smaller batches inject more\n438\tnoise into the optimization trajectory (which can help escape shallow local\n439\tminima), while larger batches yield smoother, more stable gradient estimates at\n440\tthe cost of reduced regularization effect and higher memory usage per step.\n441\t\n442\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:302 '* SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch'\n443\t// Slide: SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch\n444\t#strong[SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch]\n445\t\n446\t\n447\tAs @tab:sgdvsbgdvsminibatch shows, Table of Aspect, Batch GD, Stochastic GD,\n448\tMini-Batch GD.\n449\t\n450\t#figure(\n451\t  styled-table(\n452\t    headers: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:320 '* On-Line Learning and Gradient Descent'\n496\t// Slide: On-Line Learning and Gradient Descent\n497\t#strong[On-Line Learning and Gradient Descent]\n498\t\n499\tIn many applications, training data arrives as a #strong[continuous stream]\n500\trather than a fixed batch. The model must incorporate new observations on the\n501\tfly, updating its parameters as each example (or small group of examples)\n502\tbecomes available. This contrasts sharply with the offline setting, where the\n503\tentire dataset is collected up front and the model is trained once.\n504\t\n505\tReal-time systems make this requirement especially pressing. A deployed model\n506\tneeds to adapt to new data points without full retraining, and it must handle\n507\tvariation in the underlying process dynamics: the distribution generating the\n508\tdata may shift over time, so yesterday's optimal parameters may no longer be\n509\tadequate today.\n510\t\n511\t```graphviz\n512\tdigraph StreamModel {\n513\t    rankdir=LR;\n514\t    splines=true;\n515\t    nodesep=1.0;\n516\t    ranksep=0.50;\n517\t\n518\t    node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n519\t\n520\t    // Node styles\n521\t    DataStream [label=<Stream of data<BR/>x<SUB>i</SUB>>, fillcolor=white, shape=plaintext];\n522\t    Model      [label=\"Model\", fillcolor=\"#C6A6F4\"];\n523\t    Output     [label=<Output<BR/>y<SUB>i</SUB>>, fillcolor=white, shape=plaintext];\n524\t\n525\t    // Edges\n526\t    DataStream -> Model;\n527\t    Model -> Model [label=<w<SUB>i</SUB>>, fontsize=10];\n528\t    Model -> Output;\n529\t}\n530\t```\n531\tlabel=fig:onlinelearningandgradientdescent caption=Diagram relating Model\n532\t\n533\tStochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent are naturally\n534\t#emph[suitable for online learning], as @fig:onlinelearningandgradientdescent\n535\tillustrates. Because these methods update the model one example (or one small\n536\tbatch) at a time, they fit directly into a streaming pipeline: each incoming\n537\tobservation triggers a parameter update, after which the raw data point can be\n538\tdiscarded. The model itself serves as a \"compressed\" representation of\n539\teverything seen so far, which is valuable when storing every data point is\n540\timpractical. Consider stock market prediction, where tick-by-tick price data\n541\taccumulates at enormous volume, or training a language model on live chat data,\n542\twhere older conversations can be dropped after the model has absorbed their\n543\tsignal.\n544\t\n545\tThat said, discarding the data is generally #emph[a bad idea] whenever it can be\n546\tavoided. Once raw examples are gone, there is no way to revisit them if the\n547\tlearning rate was poorly chosen, if the model class changes, or if a subtle bug\n548\tcorrupted earlier updates. Retaining at least a representative buffer or summary\n549\tstatistics provides a safety net that pure online updates lack.\n550\t\n551\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:369 '* Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent'\n552\t// Slide: Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent\n553\t#strong[Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent]\n554\t\n555\tBatch gradient descent lends itself naturally to distributed computation because\n556\tits core operation, summing gradient contributions across the entire dataset, is\n557\tembarrassingly parallel. This makes it a good fit for the #strong[map-reduce]\n558\tparadigm, a big data framework that splits distributed computation into two\n559\tphases. In the #emph[map step], $k$ worker machines each compute partial\n560\tgradient sums over their local shard of the data. In the #emph[reduce step],\n561\tthose $k$ partial sums are sent to a single node that accumulates them into the\n562\tfull gradient, which is then used to update the model parameters. As\n563\t@fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent illustrates, the shuffle-and-sort stage\n564\troutes each worker's partial gradient to the aggregation node, which produces\n565\tthe aggregated gradient and applies it to the current model parameters. Many\n566\tlearning algorithms beyond plain gradient descent share this sum-then-update\n567\tstructure, so map-reduce serves as a general-purpose backbone for large-scale\n568\tmodel training whenever the objective decomposes into independent per-example\n569\tterms.\n570\t\n571\t```graphviz\n572\tdigraph BayesianFlow {\n573\t    splines=true;\n574\t    nodesep=1.0;\n575\t    ranksep=0.75;\n576\t\n577\t    // Operation nodes (rounded boxes)\n578\t    node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n579\t\n580\t    Map_0 [label=<Map<SUB>0</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n581\t    Map_1 [label=<Map<SUB>1</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n582\t    Map_n [label=<Map<SUB>n</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n583\t    ShuffleSort [label=\"Shuffle & Sort\", fillcolor=\"#C6A6F4\"];\n584\t    Update [label=\"Update Model\", fillcolor=\"#D2B48C\"];\n585\t\n586\t    // Variable/value nodes (plain ellipses with white background)\n587\t    node [shape=ellipse, style=filled, fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4, fillcolor=white];\n588\t\n589\t    DataShard_0  [label=<DataShard<SUB>0</SUB>>];\n590\t    DataShard_1  [label=<DataShard<SUB>1</SUB>>];\n591\t    DataShard_n  [label=<DataShard<SUB>n</SUB>>];\n592\t\n593\t    Gradient_0 [label=<Gradient<SUB>0</SUB>>];\n594\t    Gradient_1 [label=<Gradient<SUB>1</SUB>>];\n595\t    Gradient_n [label=<Gradient<SUB>n</SUB>>];\n596\t\n597\t    AggregatedGradient [label=\"Aggregated Gradient\"];\n598\t    Model [label=\"Model Parameters\"];\n599\t\n600\t    // Force ranks\n601\t    { rank=same; DataShard_0; DataShard_1; DataShard_n; }\n602\t    { rank=same; Map_0; Map_1; Map_n; }\n603\t    { rank=same; Gradient_0; Gradient_1; Gradient_n; }\n604\t\n605\t    // Edges\n606\t    DataShard_0 -> Map_0 -> Gradient_0;\n607\t    DataShard_1 -> Map_1 -> Gradient_1;\n608\t    DataShard_n -> Map_n -> Gradient_n;\n609\t\n610\t    Gradient_0 -> ShuffleSort;\n611\t    Gradient_1 -> ShuffleSort;\n612\t    Gradient_n -> ShuffleSort;\n613\t\n614\t    ShuffleSort -> AggregatedGradient;\n615\t    AggregatedGradient -> Update;\n616\t    Model -> Update -> Model;\n617\t}\n618\t```\n619\tlabel=fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent caption=Diagram relating Shuffle &\n620\tSort, Update Model, Aggregated Gradient and Model Parameters\n621\t\n622\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:435 '# Alternatives to Gradient Descent'\n623\t// Slide: Alternatives to Gradient Descent\n624\t#strong[Alternatives to Gradient Descent]\n625\t\n626\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:437 '* Coordinate Descent'\n627\t// Slide: Coordinate Descent\n628\t#strong[Coordinate Descent]\n629\t\n630\tThe core idea behind #strong[coordinate descent] is to minimize a cost function\n631\t$J(x_0, dots, x_n)$ by optimizing along one coordinate direction $x_i$ at a\n632\ttime, rather than computing all partial derivatives simultaneously. This reduces\n633\teach step to a one-dimensional optimization problem, which is often much simpler\n634\tto solve.\n635\t\n636\tThe procedure works as follows:\n637\t\n638\t+ Pick a random starting point $bold(w)^((0))$.\n639\t+ Pick a random order for the coordinates $\\{x_i\\}$.\n640\t+ Find the minimum of $J$ along the current coordinate direction (a 1D\n641\t  optimization problem).\n642\t+ Move to the next coordinate $x_(i+1)$ and repeat.\n643\t+ Continue cycling through all coordinates; the sequence of iterates\n644\t  $bold(w)^((t))$ produces monotonically decreasing values of $J$.\n645\t+ Declare convergence when a full cycle through every coordinate yields no\n646\t  further improvement.\n647\t\n648\tThe minimum found by this process is, in general, only a local minimum.\n649\tCoordinate descent avoids the cost of computing full gradients at each step,\n650\twhich can be advantageous when the number of coordinates is large or when the\n651\tper-coordinate subproblem has a closed-form solution. The tradeoff is that\n652\tprogress can be slow when the coordinates are strongly coupled, since the method\n653\tcannot take diagonal steps through the search space.\n654\t\n655\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:453 '* Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse'\n656\t// Slide: Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse\n657\t#strong[Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse]\n658\t\n659\tFor linear models, two main approaches find the optimal weight vector $vw^*$:\n660\tthe pseudo-inverse (closed-form solution) and gradient descent (iterative\n661\toptimization).\n662\t\n663\t#strong[Gradient descent] updates the weights repeatedly in the direction that\n664\treduces the loss. You choose a learning rate $eta$, then iterate until\n665\tconvergence. This requires monitoring stopping criteria and watching for\n666\toscillations, since a learning rate that is too large causes the updates to\n667\tovershoot and diverge, while one that is too small makes training painfully\n668\tslow. The key advantage of gradient descent is scalability: when the number of\n669\tfeatures $P$ is large, each iteration costs $O(N P)$ for $N$ data points, which\n670\tremains tractable even in high dimensions.\n671\t\n672\tThe #strong[pseudo-inverse] method solves for $vw^*$ directly using the normal\n673\tequations. It requires no hyperparameter selection and converges in a single\n674\tstep, which makes it appealing when it is computationally feasible. The catch is\n675\tthat it requires computing the $P times P$ matrix $(bold(X)^T bold(X))^(-1)$,\n676\tand matrix inversion has complexity $O(P^3)$. For modest feature counts this is\n677\tperfectly fine, but once $P$ reaches roughly 10,000 or more, that cubic cost\n678\tbecomes prohibitive, and gradient descent is the better choice.\n679\t\n680\tIn practice, the decision between the two comes down to the dimensionality of\n681\tthe problem: use the pseudo-inverse for smaller feature spaces where the\n682\tone-shot solution is fast, and switch to gradient descent when $P$ grows large\n683\tenough that inverting $bold(X)^T bold(X)$ is no longer practical.\n684\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"3e03a3dd-e748-4812-abec-7401348a2c93","uuid":"e540f447-cc50-43f3-ae37-8e35458b8942","timestamp":"2026-09-08T00:16:51.121Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/Users/saggese/src/umd_classes1/msml610/book/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.typ","content":"// git_hash=418671a2a-o1r timestamp=20260907_201646\n// Import AIMA style formatting and macros.\n#import \"/helpers_root/dev_scripts_helpers/typst/aima_style.typ\": (\n  aima-style, algorithm, chapter, glossary, styled-table,\n)\n// Import the custom citation/bibliography system.\n#import \"/helpers_root/dev_scripts_helpers/typst/umd_references.typ\": (\n  cite, references,\n)\n\n// Document metadata\n#set document(\n  title: \"L02.4: ML Techniques - Model Learning\",\n  author: \"MSML610: Advanced Machine Learning\",\n)\n\n// Apply the AIMA document template (page/text/heading set + show rules).\n#show: aima-style\n\n#chapter(\"L02.4: ML Techniques - Model Learning\")\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:11 '# The Optimization Problem'\n// Slide: The Optimization Problem\n#strong[The Optimization Problem]\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:13 '* Minimizing a Function'\n// Slide: Minimizing a Function\n#strong[Minimizing a Function]\n\nThe goal of optimization in machine learning is to minimize a scalar function\n$J(bold(w))$ of $P$ variables $bold(w)$. A common instance is the in-sample\nerror\n\n$ E_(i n)(bold(w)) eq.def 1/N sum_(i=1)^N e(h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i), y_i) $\n\nwhich averages the pointwise error of a hypothesis $h_(bold(w))$ over $N$\ntraining examples $(bold(x)_i, y_i)$.\n\nTwo broad strategies exist for finding the minimizer. The first is an\n#emph[analytical approach]: set the gradient of $J(bold(w))$ equal to zero and\nsolve for $bold(w)^*$ in closed form. This is elegant when it works, but many\nobjective functions do not admit a closed-form solution, or the solution is too\nexpensive to compute for large $P$. The second is a #emph[numerical approach]:\nuse an iterative method that updates $bold(w)$ step by step until $J(bold(w))$\nreaches its minimum. Gradient descent is the prototypical example. A numerical\nmethod remains applicable even when an analytical solution exists, making it the\nmore general-purpose tool, and it scales naturally to the high-dimensional\nparameter spaces encountered in modern models.\n\n@fig:gradientdescent2 illustrates how gradient descent iteratively moves toward\na minimum of the objective surface.\n\n#figure(\n  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_2.png\", width: 80%),\n  caption: [Gradient descent 2],\n  kind: \"figure\",\n  supplement: [Fig.],\n  placement: auto,\n) <fig:gradientdescent2>\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:43 '* Gradient Descent: Intuition'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent: Intuition\n#strong[Gradient Descent: Intuition]\n\nImagine standing on a hilly surface with the goal of reaching the lowest point.\nHow do you get there? At each position, you look around to assess the slope in\nevery direction, then take a step along the steepest downhill direction. You\nrepeat this process until you arrive at a point where no further descent is\npossible. This intuitive procedure is precisely what gradient descent formalizes\nfor mathematical optimization, as @fig:gradientdescent1 illustrates.\n\n#figure(\n  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_1.png\", width: 80%),\n  caption: [Gradient descent 1],\n  kind: \"figure\",\n  supplement: [Fig.],\n  placement: auto,\n) <fig:gradientdescent1>\n\n#strong[Gradient descent] is a general technique for minimizing\ntwice-differentiable functions. Starting from an initial guess, the algorithm\niteratively adjusts its parameters by moving in the direction of the negative\ngradient (the direction of steepest decrease). In the general case, gradient\ndescent converges to a #emph[local minimum], a point that is lower than all\nnearby points but not necessarily the lowest point overall. However, when the\nobjective function $J(bold(w))$ is convex, every local minimum is also the\nglobal minimum, so gradient descent is guaranteed to find the best possible\nsolution. Common models whose loss functions are convex include logistic\nregression and linear regression, which is one reason these models are so widely\nused in practice: their optimization landscape contains no misleading valleys or\nplateaus.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:73 '# Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent\n#strong[Gradient Descent]\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:75 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)\n#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (1/3)]\n\nConsider the contour plot of a loss function $E_{\"in\"}$ over weight space.\nGradient descent begins from an initial point $bold(w)(0)$, which might be\nchosen randomly or set to the origin. At each step, the algorithm moves a fixed\ndistance $eta$ (the learning rate) through weight space:\n\n$ bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) + eta hat(bold(v)) $\n\nwhere $hat(bold(v))$ is a unit vector indicating the direction of the step. The\ngoal is to choose $hat(bold(v))$ so that $E_{\"in\"}(bold(w))$ decreases as much\nas possible.\n\nTo see which direction accomplishes this, examine the change in the error:\n\n$\n  Delta E_{\"in\"} &= E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t + 1)) - E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t)) \\\n  &= E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t) + eta hat(bold(v))) - E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t)) \\\n  &approx eta nabla E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v)) + O(eta^2)\n$\n\nThe last line follows from a first-order Taylor expansion around $bold(w)(t)$.\nStandard gradient descent retains only the $O(eta)$ term and discards\nhigher-order contributions. Because $eta$ is a positive scalar, making\n$Delta E_{\"in\"}$ as negative as possible requires choosing $hat(bold(v))$ to\nminimize the inner product $nabla E_{\"in\"}(bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v))$; the unit\nvector that achieves this points in the direction opposite the gradient. More\nadvanced methods such as #emph[conjugate gradient] retain the $O(eta^2)$ term as\nwell, which allows them to account for curvature information and often converge\nfaster, though at a higher per-step cost.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:107 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)\n#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (2/3)]\n\nThe change in the in-sample error $E_(i n)$ when moving along a unit direction\n$hat(bold(v))$ is approximately\n\n$ Delta E_(i n) approx eta nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t))^T hat(bold(v)) $\n\nThis expression is a first-order Taylor approximation: the error shift is\nproportional to the learning rate $eta$ and to how well the step direction\n$hat(bold(v))$ aligns with the gradient. The scalar product $Delta E_(i n)$\nreaches its most negative value when $hat(bold(v))$ points exactly opposite to\nthe gradient, that is, when\n\n$\n  hat(bold(v)) = - frac(nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)), \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|)\n$\n\nAt that choice the change equals $- eta \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|$, the\nsteepest possible decrease for a step of size $eta$.\n\nSubstituting this optimal direction back into the weight update gives the full\nrule for the #strong[change in weights]:\n\n$\n  Delta bold(w) &= bold(w)(t + 1) - bold(w)(t) \\\n  &= eta hat(bold(v)) \\\n  &= - eta frac(nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)), \\| nabla E_(i n) (bold(w)(t)) \\|)\n$\n\nEach iteration therefore moves the weight vector a fixed distance $eta$ in\nwhichever direction reduces the error most steeply. The method is called\n#strong[gradient descent] precisely because it descends along the gradient of\nthe objective function, following the locally steepest downhill path at every\nstep.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:133 '* Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)\n#strong[Gradient Descent with Fixed Learning Rate (3/3)]\n\nThe gradient descent update formula specifies how each component of the weight\nvector changes at every step. The full vector update is\n\n$\n  bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) - eta frac(nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t)), \\|nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t))\\|)\n$\n\nand the corresponding per-coordinate form for the $j$-th weight is\n\n$\n  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - eta frac(1, \\|nabla E_(i n)(bold(w)(t))\\|) frac(partial E_(i n)(bold(w)), partial w_j)\n$\n\nEach weight moves in the direction that locally reduces the in-sample error,\nscaled by the learning rate $eta$ and normalized by the gradient's magnitude. A\ncritical detail is that the update of all components must be\n#emph[simultaneous]: every partial derivative is evaluated at the current point\n$bold(w)(t)$ before any component is changed, so no single coordinate's new\nvalue contaminates the computation of another's update within the same step.\n\nAn #strong[iteration] of gradient descent refers to one complete application of\nthis update rule, producing a new weight vector from the current one. Counting\niterations gives a natural measure of computational effort and is the basis for\nconvergence criteria and stopping conditions.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:153 '* Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria\n#strong[Gradient Descent: Stopping Criteria]\n\nWhen should gradient descent stop? In theory, the algorithm terminates when the\nchange in the in-sample error reaches zero, $Delta E_(\"in\") = bold(0)$. In\npractice, however, this exact condition may never be satisfied numerically due\nto finite floating-point precision and the iterative nature of the updates. Two\npractical stopping criteria are commonly used instead:\n\n- #emph[Threshold on variation]: stop when the change in $E_(\"in\")$ falls below\n  a small threshold, $Delta E_(\"in\") < theta$.\n- #emph[Iteration budget]: stop after a predetermined number of iterations,\n  regardless of whether full convergence has been reached.\n\nMonitoring the optimization process also differs between theory and practice. In\ntheory, gradient descent requires only the derivatives of the cost function\n$J(bold(w))$ to determine each update step. In practice, it is wise to\nperiodically recompute the cost function $J(bold(w))$ itself and verify that it\nis actually decreasing. If the cost plateaus or begins to increase, that signals\na problem: the learning rate may be too large, causing the iterates to\novershoot, or the algorithm may have reached a region of the loss surface where\nthe gradient provides poor guidance. Periodically logging $J(bold(w))$ provides\na simple but effective diagnostic for catching these issues early.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:167 '# Tuning Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Tuning Gradient Descent\n#strong[Tuning Gradient Descent]\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:169 '* Choosing the Learning Rate'\n// Slide: Choosing the Learning Rate\n#strong[Choosing the Learning Rate]\n\nConsider a one-dimensional convex function whose minimum we seek via gradient\ndescent. The behavior of the algorithm depends critically on the choice of\nlearning rate $eta$.\n\nWhen $eta$ is too small, the linear approximation of $E_(i n)$ remains effective\nat each step, so every update does move downhill, but the steps are tiny and\nconvergence to the minimum requires a large number of iterations.\n@fig:gradientdescent3a illustrates this slow, cautious trajectory.\n\n#figure(\n  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3a.png\", width: 80%),\n  caption: [Gradient descent 3a],\n  kind: \"figure\",\n  supplement: [Fig.],\n  placement: auto,\n) <fig:gradientdescent3a>\n\nWhen $eta$ is too large, the linear approximation breaks down because\nhigher-order terms in the Taylor expansion dominate the actual function values.\nInstead of descending smoothly, the iterates overshoot the minimum and bounce\nback and forth across the valley, potentially diverging altogether.\n@fig:gradientdescent3b shows this oscillatory behavior.\n\n#figure(\n  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3b.png\", width: 80%),\n  caption: [Gradient descent 3b],\n  kind: \"figure\",\n  supplement: [Fig.],\n  placement: auto,\n) <fig:gradientdescent3b>\n\nA natural idea is to vary $eta$ over the course of optimization. Starting with a\nlarger learning rate lets the algorithm make rapid initial progress, and then\ngradually reducing $eta$ as a function of the iteration count allows it to\nsettle into a tighter neighborhood of the minimum. Smaller learning rates in\nlater stages can even help the optimizer find a better local minimum in\nnon-convex landscapes. The tradeoff is that a learning-rate schedule introduces\nan additional hyperparameter (or family of hyperparameters, such as a decay rate\nand a decay schedule) that must itself be tuned, adding complexity to the\ntraining pipeline. @fig:gradientdescent3c depicts the effect of a well-chosen\nadaptive schedule, where early large steps give way to finer adjustments near\nthe optimum.\n\n#figure(\n  image(\"../lectures_source/figures/L02.4.Gradient_descent_3c.png\", width: 80%),\n  caption: [Gradient descent 3c],\n  kind: \"figure\",\n  supplement: [Fig.],\n  placement: auto,\n) <fig:gradientdescent3c>\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:202 '* Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate\n#strong[Gradient Descent with Variable Learning Rate]\n\nWhen using #strong[gradient descent with a fixed learning rate], every update\nmoves the same distance through weight space regardless of how steep the surface\nis. The update rule normalizes the gradient so that only its direction matters:\n\n$ Delta bold(w) = - eta frac(nabla J, \\|nabla J\\|) $\n\nThis keeps the step size constant at $eta$, but that uniformity creates a\nproblem. On steep regions of the loss surface, a fixed step may be too small,\nmaking progress painfully slow. Near a minimum, where the surface flattens out,\nthat same fixed step may be too large, causing the optimizer to overshoot and\nbounce back and forth across the valley instead of settling in.\n\nTo converge quickly, the learning rate should adapt to the local geometry. The\noptimizer should take large steps when the gradient is large (the surface is\nsteep and far from a minimum) and small steps when the gradient is small (the\nsurface is nearly flat and close to a minimum). In other words, the ideal\nlearning rate is proportional to the gradient magnitude: $eta prop \\|nabla J\\|$.\n\n#strong[Gradient descent with a variable learning rate] achieves exactly this by\ndropping the normalization and using the raw gradient directly:\n\n$ Delta bold(w) = - eta nabla J $\n\nBecause the gradient vector $nabla J$ is not divided by its own norm, its\nmagnitude naturally scales the step size. When the surface is steep,\n$\\|nabla J\\|$ is large and the update moves farther; when the surface is gentle,\n$\\|nabla J\\|$ is small and the update shrinks. The scalar $eta$ still controls\nthe overall scale, but the gradient's magnitude now acts as a built-in adaptive\nfactor. This simple change gives the optimizer the variable-rate behavior needed\nfor efficient convergence: aggressive movement far from the optimum and cautious\nrefinement near it.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:222 '* Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent\n#strong[Feature Scaling in Gradient Descent]\n\nUnscaled features distort the error surface. When one feature ranges from 1 to\n1000 while another ranges from 0.01 to 1, the level sets of $E_\"in\" (bold(w))$\nbecome elongated ellipses rather than circles. A single learning rate cannot\nserve both directions well: it is too large along the steep, short-axis\ndirection (causing the updates to overshoot and bounce) and too small along the\nflat, long-axis direction (causing the optimizer to crawl). The result is slow,\nunstable convergence that zigzags across the narrow valley instead of heading\nstraight for the minimum.\n\nThe fix is to rescale every feature so that all of them span comparable ranges\nbefore training begins. Two common choices are #emph[min-max scaling], which\nmaps each feature to the interval $[0, 1]$, and #emph[standardization], which\ncenters each feature at zero with unit variance. Either approach reshapes the\nelongated ellipses into something much closer to circles, so a single learning\nrate works reasonably well in every direction and gradient descent converges\nfaster and more smoothly.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:236 '# Scaling to Large Datasets'\n// Slide: Scaling to Large Datasets\n#strong[Scaling to Large Datasets]\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:238 '* Issues with Batch Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Issues with Batch Gradient Descent\n#strong[Issues with Batch Gradient Descent]\n\nConsider the squared error over $N$ training samples, defined as\n\n$\n  E_(i n)(bold(w)) triangleq 1 / N sum_(i=1)^N (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i) - y_i)^2\n$\n\nThis measures the average discrepancy between the hypothesis $h_(bold(w))$ and\nthe observed targets across the entire dataset. Minimizing it drives the model\ntoward a set of weights that fits the training data well.\n\n#strong[Batch Gradient Descent (BGD)] updates the weight vector by stepping in\nthe direction opposite to the normalized gradient of the in-sample error:\n\n$ bold(w)(t + 1) = bold(w)(t) - eta frac(nabla E_(i n), \\|nabla E_(i n)\\|) $\n\nWriting out the coordinate-level update for the squared error loss makes the\ncomputation concrete. Each weight component $w_j$ changes according to\n\n$\n  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - eta frac(2, N) sum_(i=1)^N (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i) - y_i) frac(partial h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_i), partial w_j)\n$\n\nThe inner sum sweeps over every training example, accumulating the product of\nthe current residual and the local sensitivity of the hypothesis to $w_j$. Only\nafter that full pass does the algorithm take a single step.\n\nThat full-dataset requirement is the chief drawback of batch gradient descent.\nWhen $N$ is large (say, $N = 10^6$), every single weight update demands a\ngradient evaluation that touches all $10^6$ examples, making each iteration\ncomputationally expensive. The entire dataset must also reside in memory at\nonce, which can be prohibitive for large-scale problems. These costs motivate\nthe stochastic and mini-batch variants discussed next, which trade a noisier\ngradient estimate for dramatically cheaper per-step computation.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:263 '* Stochastic Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Stochastic Gradient Descent\n#strong[Stochastic Gradient Descent]\n\n#strong[Stochastic Gradient Descent] (SGD) updates the weights using only a\nsingle training example chosen at random, rather than computing the gradient\nover the entire dataset. This makes each update far cheaper, which is especially\nvaluable when the training set is large.\n\nThe procedure works as follows:\n\n1. Pick one example $(bold(x)_n, y_n)$ at random from the training set.\n2. Compute the gradient of the loss for that single example,\n  $nabla e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n)$, and form the weight update\n  $Delta bold(w) = -eta nabla e$.\n3. Apply the update to each weight:\n\n$\n  w_j (t + 1) = w_j (t) - 2 eta (h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_t) - y_t) frac(partial h_(bold(w))(bold(x)_t), partial w_j)\n$\n\nBecause each step relies on a single randomly selected example, the path SGD\ntraces through weight space is noisy: it does not follow the smooth trajectory\nof batch gradient descent but instead oscillates, sometimes moving away from the\noptimum before correcting course. Near a local minimum the updates do not settle\ncleanly; they bounce around the basin rather than converging to a fixed point.\n\nDespite this apparent randomness, SGD works because the gradient $nabla e$ is a\nfunction of a random variable $bold(x)_n$, and its expected value equals the\nfull-batch gradient. Concretely:\n\n$\n  bb(E)[nabla e] = frac(1, N) sum nabla e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n) = nabla frac(1, N) sum e(h(bold(x)_n), y_n) = nabla E_(\"in\")\n$\n\nIn other words, although any single SGD step may point in a direction that\ndiffers from the true gradient, on average the steps point the same way as the\nbatch gradient. Over many iterations the random deviations cancel out, and the\nalgorithm makes steady progress toward a minimum of the in-sample error. The\noscillation that is a drawback in the short term actually confers a benefit: the\nnoise helps SGD escape shallow local minima that batch descent might get trapped\nin, often leading to solutions that generalize better.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:294 '* Mini-Batch Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent\n#strong[Mini-Batch Gradient Descent]\n\n#strong[Mini-batch gradient descent] brings together characteristics of both\n#emph[batch] and #emph[stochastic gradient descent]. Rather than computing the\ngradient over the entire training set (as in batch gradient descent) or from a\nsingle example (as in stochastic gradient descent), mini-batch gradient descent\nuses a subset of $b$ examples to compute each update to the current weight\nvector. Here $b$ is called the #emph[batch size], and common choices are\n$b = 32$ or $b = 64$. This middle ground reduces the variance of parameter\nupdates compared to the single-sample stochastic approach, while remaining far\nmore computationally tractable per step than a full-batch computation.\nMini-batch updates also benefit from hardware-level parallelism on modern GPUs,\nwhich are optimized for matrix operations on moderately sized batches. The\nchoice of batch size introduces its own tradeoff: smaller batches inject more\nnoise into the optimization trajectory (which can help escape shallow local\nminima), while larger batches yield smoother, more stable gradient estimates at\nthe cost of reduced regularization effect and higher memory usage per step.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:302 '* SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch'\n// Slide: SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch\n#strong[SGD vs BGD vs Mini-Batch]\n\n\nAs @tab:sgdvsbgdvsminibatch shows, Table of Aspect, Batch GD, Stochastic GD,\nMini-Batch GD.\n\n#figure(\n  styled-table(\n    headers: (\"Aspect\", \"Batch GD\", \"Stochastic GD\", \"Mini-Batch GD\"),\n    rows: (\n      (\n        \"Computation\",\n        \"Uses all examples\",\n        \"One random example at a time\",\n        \"A random subset (b examples) at a time\",\n      ),\n      (\n and Gradient Descent\n#strong[On-Line Learning and Gradient Descent]\n\nIn many applications, training data arrives as a #strong[continuous stream]\nrather than a fixed batch. The model must incorporate new observations on the\nfly, updating its parameters as each example (or small group of examples)\nbecomes available. This contrasts sharply with the offline setting, where the\nentire dataset is collected up front and the model is trained once.\n\nReal-time systems make this requirement especially pressing. A deployed model\nneeds to adapt to new data points without full retraining, and it must handle\nvariation in the underlying process dynamics: the distribution generating the\ndata may shift over time, so yesterday's optimal parameters may no longer be\nadequate today.\n\n```graphviz\ndigraph StreamModel {\n    rankdir=LR;\n    splines=true;\n    nodesep=1.0;\n    ranksep=0.50;\n\n    node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n\n    // Node styles\n    DataStream [label=<Stream of data<BR/>x<SUB>i</SUB>>, fillcolor=white, shape=plaintext];\n    Model      [label=\"Model\", fillcolor=\"#C6A6F4\"];\n    Output     [label=<Output<BR/>y<SUB>i</SUB>>, fillcolor=white, shape=plaintext];\n\n    // Edges\n    DataStream -> Model;\n    Model -> Model [label=<w<SUB>i</SUB>>, fontsize=10];\n    Model -> Output;\n}\n```\nlabel=fig:onlinelearningandgradientdescent caption=Diagram relating Model\n\nStochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent are naturally\n#emph[suitable for online learning], as @fig:onlinelearningandgradientdescent\nillustrates. Because these methods update the model one example (or one small\nbatch) at a time, they fit directly into a streaming pipeline: each incoming\nobservation triggers a parameter update, after which the raw data point can be\ndiscarded. The model itself serves as a \"compressed\" representation of\neverything seen so far, which is valuable when storing every data point is\nimpractical. Consider stock market prediction, where tick-by-tick price data\naccumulates at enormous volume, or training a language model on live chat data,\nwhere older conversations can be dropped after the model has absorbed their\nsignal.\n\nThat said, discarding the data is generally #emph[a bad idea] whenever it can be\navoided. Once raw examples are gone, there is no way to revisit them if the\nlearning rate was poorly chosen, if the model class changes, or if a subtle bug\ncorrupted earlier updates. Retaining at least a representative buffer or summary\nstatistics provides a safety net that pure online updates lack.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:369 '* Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent\n#strong[Map-Reduce for Batch Gradient Descent]\n\nBatch gradient descent lends itself naturally to distributed computation because\nits core operation, summing gradient contributions across the entire dataset, is\nembarrassingly parallel. This makes it a good fit for the #strong[map-reduce]\nparadigm, a big data framework that splits distributed computation into two\nphases. In the #emph[map step], $k$ worker machines each compute partial\ngradient sums over their local shard of the data. In the #emph[reduce step],\nthose $k$ partial sums are sent to a single node that accumulates them into the\nfull gradient, which is then used to update the model parameters. As\n@fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent illustrates, the shuffle-and-sort stage\nroutes each worker's partial gradient to the aggregation node, which produces\nthe aggregated gradient and applies it to the current model parameters. Many\nlearning algorithms beyond plain gradient descent share this sum-then-update\nstructure, so map-reduce serves as a general-purpose backbone for large-scale\nmodel training whenever the objective decomposes into independent per-example\nterms.\n\n```graphviz\ndigraph BayesianFlow {\n    splines=true;\n    nodesep=1.0;\n    ranksep=0.75;\n\n    // Operation nodes (rounded boxes)\n    node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n\n    Map_0 [label=<Map<SUB>0</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n    Map_1 [label=<Map<SUB>1</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n    Map_n [label=<Map<SUB>n</SUB><BR/>Compute Gradient>, fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n    ShuffleSort [label=\"Shuffle & Sort\", fillcolor=\"#C6A6F4\"];\n    Update [label=\"Update Model\", fillcolor=\"#D2B48C\"];\n\n    // Variable/value nodes (plain ellipses with white background)\n    node [shape=ellipse, style=filled, fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4, fillcolor=white];\n\n    DataShard_0  [label=<DataShard<SUB>0</SUB>>];\n    DataShard_1  [label=<DataShard<SUB>1</SUB>>];\n    DataShard_n  [label=<DataShard<SUB>n</SUB>>];\n\n    Gradient_0 [label=<Gradient<SUB>0</SUB>>];\n    Gradient_1 [label=<Gradient<SUB>1</SUB>>];\n    Gradient_n [label=<Gradient<SUB>n</SUB>>];\n\n    AggregatedGradient [label=\"Aggregated Gradient\"];\n    Model [label=\"Model Parameters\"];\n\n    // Force ranks\n    { rank=same; DataShard_0; DataShard_1; DataShard_n; }\n    { rank=same; Map_0; Map_1; Map_n; }\n    { rank=same; Gradient_0; Gradient_1; Gradient_n; }\n\n    // Edges\n    DataShard_0 -> Map_0 -> Gradient_0;\n    DataShard_1 -> Map_1 -> Gradient_1;\n    DataShard_n -> Map_n -> Gradient_n;\n\n    Gradient_0 -> ShuffleSort;\n    Gradient_1 -> ShuffleSort;\n    Gradient_n -> ShuffleSort;\n\n    ShuffleSort -> AggregatedGradient;\n    AggregatedGradient -> Update;\n    Model -> Update -> Model;\n}\n```\nlabel=fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent caption=Diagram relating Shuffle &\nSort, Update Model, Aggregated Gradient and Model Parameters\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:435 '# Alternatives to Gradient Descent'\n// Slide: Alternatives to Gradient Descent\n#strong[Alternatives to Gradient Descent]\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:437 '* Coordinate Descent'\n// Slide: Coordinate Descent\n#strong[Coordinate Descent]\n\nThe core idea behind #strong[coordinate descent] is to minimize a cost function\n$J(x_0, dots, x_n)$ by optimizing along one coordinate direction $x_i$ at a\ntime, rather than computing all partial derivatives simultaneously. This reduces\neach step to a one-dimensional optimization problem, which is often much simpler\nto solve.\n\nThe procedure works as follows:\n\n+ Pick a random starting point $bold(w)^((0))$.\n+ Pick a random order for the coordinates $\\{x_i\\}$.\n+ Find the minimum of $J$ along the current coordinate direction (a 1D\n  optimization problem).\n+ Move to the next coordinate $x_(i+1)$ and repeat.\n+ Continue cycling through all coordinates; the sequence of iterates\n  $bold(w)^((t))$ produces monotonically decreasing values of $J$.\n+ Declare convergence when a full cycle through every coordinate yields no\n  further improvement.\n\nThe minimum found by this process is, in general, only a local minimum.\nCoordinate descent avoids the cost of computing full gradients at each step,\nwhich can be advantageous when the number of coordinates is large or when the\nper-coordinate subproblem has a closed-form solution. The tradeoff is that\nprogress can be slow when the coordinates are strongly coupled, since the method\ncannot take diagonal steps through the search space.\n\n// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.4-ML_Techniques_Model_Learning.smd:453 '* Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse'\n// Slide: Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse\n#strong[Gradient Descent vs Pseudo-Inverse]\n\nFor linear models, two main approaches find the optimal weight vector $vw^*$:\nthe pseudo-inverse (closed-form solution) and gradient descent (iterative\noptimization).\n\n#strong[Gradient descent] updates the weights repeatedly in the direction that\nreduces the loss. You choose a learning rate $eta$, then iterate until\nconvergence. This requires monitoring stopping criteria and watching for\noscillations, since a learning rate that is too large causes the updates to\novershoot and diverge, while one that is too small makes training painfully\nslow. The key advantage of gradient descent is scalability: when the number of\nfeatures $P$ is large, each iteration costs $O(N P)$ for $N$ data points, which\nremains tractable even in high dimensions.\n\nThe #strong[pseudo-inverse] method solves for $vw^*$ directly using the normal\nequations. It requires no hyperparameter selection and converges in a single\nstep, which makes it appealing when it is computationally feasible. The catch is\nthat it requires computing the $P times P$ matrix $(bold(X)^T bold(X))^(-1)$,\nand matrix inversion has complexity $O(P^3)$. For modest feature counts this is\nperfectly fine, but once $P$ reaches roughly 10,000 or more, that cubic cost\nbecomes prohibitive, and gradient descent is the better choice.\n\nIn practice, the decision between the two comes down to the dimensionality of\nthe problem: use the pseudo-inverse for smaller feature spaces where the\none-shot solution is fast, and switch to gradient descent when $P$ grows large\nenough that inverting $bold(X)^T bold(X)$ is no longer practical.\n","numLines":684,"startLine":1,"totalLines":684}}}

This makes it a good fit for the #strong[map-reduce]\n570\tparadigm, a big data framework that splits distributed computation into two\n571\tphases. In the #emph[map step], $k$ worker machines each compute partial\n572\tgradient sums over their local shard of the data. In the #emph[reduce step],\n573\tthose $k$ partial sums are sent to a single node that accumulates them into the\n574\tfull gradient, which is then used to update the model parameters. As\n575\t@fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent illustrates, the shuffle-and-sort stage\n576\troutes each worker's partial gradient to the aggregation node, which produces\n577\tthe aggregated gradient and applies it to the current model parameters. Many\n578\tlearning algorithms beyond plain gradient descent share this sum-then-update\n579\tstructure, so map-reduce serves as a general-purpose backbone for large-scale\n580\tmodel training Because these methods update the model one example (or one small\nbatch) at a time, they fit directly into a streaming pipeline: each incoming\nobservation triggers a parameter update, after which the raw data point can be\ndiscarded. The model itself serves as a \"compressed\" representation of\neverything seen so far, which is valuable when storing every data point is\nimpractical. Consider stock market prediction, where tick-by-tick price data\naccumulates at enormous volume, or training a language model on live chat data,\nwhere older conversations can be dropped after the model has absorbed their\nsignal.\n\nThat said, discarding the data is generally #emph[a bad idea] whenever it can be\navoided. This makes it a good fit for the #strong[map-reduce]\nparadigm, a big data framework that splits distributed computation into two\nphases. In the #emph[map step], $k$ worker machines each compute partial\ngradient sums over their local shard of the data. In the #emph[reduce step],\nthose $k$ partial sums are sent to a single node that accumulates them into the\nfull gradient, which is then used to update the model parameters. As\n@fig:mapreduceforbatchgradientdescent illustrates, the shuffle-and-sort stage\nroutes each worker's partial gradient to the aggregation node, which produces\nthe aggregated gradient and applies it to the current model parameters.
